clock_fraction_45: South/East German and Austrian toward-the-hour quarters (REGIONAL): a bare
"dreiviertel <H>" names three quarters of the way toward hour H, i.e.
08:15 and "halb neun" == 08:30. Western/northern German never uses these bare
forms (it says "viertel nach acht" / "viertel vor neun", the CLOCKDIR path),
so enabling the bare quarters only ADDS readings for strings that were
unparsed before -- no collision with the "nach"/"vor" forms.
Source: Bastian Sick, "Zwiebelfisch: Von Viertel nach acht bis viertel neun"
(Spiegel Online / Der Dativ ist dem Genitiv sein Tod, Bd. 3).
clock_meridiem_am: "früh" after a clock names the morning: DWDS, "früh", Bedeutung 2: "am

clock_meridiem_am_night: "nachts" reads on the am half of the 12-hour clock ("drei nachts" is 03:00).
Over an explicit 24-hour clock it keeps 18:00-23:59 as written ("23:30
nachts"): the night starts at nightfall, not at midnight.

daypart_nacht_de: Band boundaries: Unicode CLDR 47 Day Period Rules, locale de
gives Vormittag as the "Zeit zwischen Morgen und Mittag".
The Nacht is the small hours of the named day; the Abend holds the
evening through to midnight on its own.
daypart_vormittag_de: Band boundaries: Unicode CLDR 47 Day Period Rules, locale de
gives Vormittag as the "Zeit zwischen Morgen und Mittag".
German splits what English runs together as one morning, and Vormittag
is the half English has no word for at all.

marker_clock_lead: Words that open a clock time and belong to it. They fold only in front of
a number, a clock time, a clock fraction or a clock landmark.
Each word is shown opening a clock time on the page named in brackets,
um: Wiktionary "um": "at, by (when relating to time): Um acht Uhr reisen wir ab" [de-um.wikitext.txt]
marker_counted_noun: Nouns that count people or things a clock never takes: a bare hour behind a
clock preposition and directly before one of them is a count ("wave at 5
people").  Each word is quoted from its Wiktionary Noun entry
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/<word>); the fetched pages are kept with the audit.

marker_date_lead: Words that open a date or a clock time and belong to it.
Each word is shown opening a time or date phrase on the page named in brackets,
am: de.Wiktionary "am": "[1] Angabe eines Zeitpunkts - wann? ... am Donnerstag, am 1.11.2005" [dewikt-am.wikitext.txt]
an: Wiktionary "an": "temporal, with days or times of day: on; in; at" [de-an.wikitext.txt]
im: de.Wiktionary "im": "[1] zeitlich: Position innerhalb einer genannten Zeitspanne ... Im April blühen die Anemonen." [dewikt-im.wikitext.txt]
marker_date_lead_dative: Determiners in the dative that make a this-phrase take its lead word: "an diesem Donnerstag".
Before a calendar date the determiner folds with its lead word: "an diesem 31. Januar".
DWDS, "an": "2. zeitlich a) ... Grammatik: mit Dativ. Beispiele: das Wetter an diesem" [de-an-dwds.txt]
marker_date_lead_no_deixis: Lead words that do not open a time expression that begins with this, next or last and has no
determiner in the dative ("ruf mich an nächsten Freitag", "mach das Licht an nächste Woche").
"an" governs the dative in a time phrase, so a bare accusative phrase takes no preposition and the
"an" before it belongs to the verb (anrufen, anmachen).
Because German lists determiners in marker_date_lead_dative.voc, "an" also does not open a bare
weekday, daypart or period: the time phrase is "am Montag" (de.Wiktionary "am": "[1] Angabe eines
Zeitpunkts - wann? ... am Donnerstag" [dewikt-am.wikitext.txt]), so the "an" of "ruf mich an Montag"
and "denk an Montag" belongs to the verb.
Duden, "an": "zur Angabe des Zeitpunkts. Grammatik: mit Dativ. an einem Wintermorgen, an diesem 31. Januar" [de-an-duden.txt]
DWDS, "an": "2. zeitlich a) ... Grammatik: mit Dativ. Beispiele: das Wetter an diesem, am nächsten Tag" [de-an-dwds.txt]
marker_during: "im" (in + dem) is the standard frame for a calendar month
marker_from: German range "from" lead (von/vom/ab A bis B).
"vom": Duden s.v. "von" -- "vom" is the fused form of "von dem" and is the
ordinary temporal range opener paired with "bis" ("vom 3. bis 10. Juli").
marker_last: German "last/previous" determiner.  Besides "letzte", everyday German uses
the past weekday; all three take the regular attributive-adjective endings
(strong/weak/mixed), so the inflected forms are listed in full.
marker_ordlast: German "last" ordinal determiner (attributive adjective, all endings).
"der letzte Montag im Mai" = the last Monday of May.  Duden, Flexion von "letzter".
marker_this: Source: Duden, Die Grammatik (9th ed. 2016): "diesem" is the dative singular of "dieser" ("an diesem Donnerstag").
marker_week_num: The plural is NOT a week-number surface: a German week number is always
singular ("die 2. Woche", "KW 2", "Kalenderwoche 2"), and the plural names
a COUNT of weeks. Listing it let the ordinal order read the bare counted
length "2 wochen" as calendar week 2, answering a date six months before
